summary: This program builds a list of Book objects and then walks through it to collect every book whose genre is Fantasy into a second list, which it prints. It shows the standard pattern for filtering a collection: loop, test, and copy the matches into a new list.

lines.text: ArrayList is the everyday, resizable implementation of a list, and it must be imported before you can create one.
List is the interface that describes what a list can do; declaring variables with it keeps your code free to swap in a different implementation later.
The variable's type is the List interface while the object created is an ArrayList, and the angle brackets promise that only Book objects will go in.

lines.code: Book sherlock = new Book("The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes", "Arthur Conan Doyle", "Mystery");
lines.text: Each book is built once as an object holding its title, author, and genre together, instead of three loose strings.
add appends the object to the end of the list, so the list grows as you go without you ever setting a size.
A second, empty list is the destination for the filter results; the original list is never modified.
This enhanced for loop hands you each Book in turn, which is all you need when you are only reading the list.
equalsIgnoreCase compares the text of the two strings while ignoring capitalization, so "fantasy" and "Fantasy" both match. Use it instead of == , which compares object identity rather than contents.
Only matching books are copied across, and both lists now refer to the same Book objects rather than to copies of them.
A second loop over the filtered list keeps the searching and the reporting as two clearly separate steps.
Passing an object to println calls its toString method, which is why Book needs a readable toString of its own.
